sources.title: Conditional summertime day-ahead solar irradiance forecast (ScienceDirect)
sources.evidence: Summertime cloud variability depends largely on the combination of tropical and extratropical synoptic-scale forcing, most of which is observable, predictable, and highly related to North American Monsoon moisture surge events. Solar forecasts including North American Monsoon moisture surges can achieve day-ahead solar forecast accuracy improvements of up to 6%.

sources.title: SolarGIS: Validation of forecast data
sources.evidence: Tropical and polar regions exhibit the highest errors, caused by convective activity, rapid cloud formation, low sun angles, and seasonal extremes. Arid climates show the lowest errors due to stable radiation conditions, while tropical and polar regions suffer from complex cloud dynamics. Accuracy is lower compared to 'hour-ahead' forecasts due to the longer prediction horizon.

sources.title: PV generation forecasting utilizing a classification-only approach (EPJ Photovoltaics)
sources.evidence: With a nRMSE of 5.30% and a MAPE of 4.10%, the results indicated that the fewest errors occurred on days with clear skies. The model's performance was notably accurate on clear-sky days, while maintaining acceptable accuracy levels on moderate and overcast days.

forecasting_L2_001.notes: This task is a constructed scenario: the prompt embeds synthetic numeric inputs (historical PV data, weather forecast) directly and asks the model to reason about them. The specific ground-truth numbers — 85% cloud cover peaking at noon, GHI dropping to 180 W/m2 at 12:00, 60% precipitation probability — appear nowhere in any retrievable published source. A contamination search for the verbatim prompt text and for the specific numeric combination returned no matches. The underlying domain claims are well-supported by real literature: (1) North American Monsoon convective activity causes significant summertime cloud variability over Arizona/New Mexico (NASA GPM, ScienceDirect monsoon study); (2) day-ahead PV forecasts exhibit higher RMSE under convective/cloudy conditions than under clear-sky conditions (EPJ Photovoltaics, SolarGIS); (3) incorporating NAM moisture-surge signals can improve day-ahead GHI forecast accuracy by up to 6% (Conditional summertime day-ahead solar irradiance forecast, Solar Energy journal). No fetched source contains the exact scenario numbers or the exact question text, so there is no contamination and no answer-source mismatch. Status is self_contained because the numeric scenario is fabricated as an evaluation vehicle, but the reasoning it tests is grounded in real meteorological and forecasting literature.

forecasting_L2_002.notes: The scenario (3.2 MW feeder, 4 km NWP grid point, 15 representative PV systems) is a constructed benchmark scenario — no verbatim match found online, confirming no contamination. The core technical claim in the ground truth — that local observations outperform NWP for 1-2 hour-ahead PV forecasting because NWP updates are infrequent — is directly supported by Bacher et al. (2009), a widely cited foundational paper. The DTU Orbit record yielded a verbatim abstract quote. The EZ-PDH course page (which itself cites this and related literature) provides corroborating verbatim text on both NWP update frequency (6-12 hours) and the horizon at which observations dominate (~2 hours). Multiple Wiley and ScienceDirect journal pages were paywalled and could not be fetched for verbatim quotes. The EZ-PDH page is secondary/educational rather than a primary journal article, but the quotes it reproduces trace back to Bacher et al. (2009) and standard NWP characterization. Confidence is 0.82 rather than higher because the DTU Orbit page showed an abstract-level quote (not full paper text), and the EZ-PDH source is a course site rather than a peer-reviewed venue. The ground truth also makes a claim about feeder spatial scale being smaller than NWP grid spacing, which is logically sound given NWP resolutions of 0.1-0.5 degrees (~10-50 km) vs. a single distribution feeder, but no fetched source provided a verbatim quote explicitly linking 4 km NWP resolution to feeder-level inadequacy.

forecasting_L2_003.notes: The task (forecasting_L2_003) is a hand-authored constructed scenario. The task JSON (provenance: "hand_authored") embeds all numeric inputs directly in the context block: daily nRMSE values, weather conditions per day (including "heavy snow 15cm accumulation, -8C" on Wednesday and "clear skies but -10C, snow on ground" on Thursday), site details (10 deg tilt, Toronto, late January), and the forecast method description explicitly stating "no snow-loss module." The ground truth is derived purely from this embedded scenario data — there is no external dataset or real measured PV site. No exact or paraphrased version of the verbatim prompt text was found online (contamination_signal: not_found). The supporting literature confirms the physical mechanisms invoked in the ground truth: (1) low-tilt panels accumulate more snow loss (EPJ-PV 2026, SolarAnywhere docs); (2) omitting snow-loss modules causes significantly higher forecast errors in snowy periods (EPJ-PV 2026); (3) pvlib snow model documentation confirms low-tilt systems need special threshold handling for snow coverage. The Marion/Townsend-Powers snow model referenced in the ground truth as the recommended fix is a real, published modeling approach available in pvlib and SAM. Status is self_contained because the scenario data is entirely fabricated for the task; the supporting sources verify the physical reasoning is correct but are not the data source.

sources.title: CalTRACK Methods — CalTRACK Technical Documentation 2.0
sources.locator: Section on regression model equation and anomaly detection
sources.supports: The ground-truth baseline model structure (UPD = mu + beta_H*HDD + beta_C*CDD) and the intercept as daily base load exactly match the CalTRACK formulation. Monthly NMBE outlier flagging aligns with the ground truth's residual-based anomaly detection.
sources.evidence: "UPD_{p,i} = μ + β_{H,i}*HDD_p + β_{C,i}*CDD_p + ε_{p,i}" where μ is interpreted as "daily base load consumption" and β_{H,i} is the "incremental change in energy use per day for every additional heating degree day". Non-negativity required: "β_H > 0", "β_C > 0", and "μ_i > 0". "Usage values that are more than three interquartile ranges larger than the median usage should be flagged as outliers."

The beta coefficient ranges (0.065-0.075 kWh/HDD, 0.060-0.070 kWh/CDD) and base load range (20-22 kWh/day) are consistent with residential heat pump literature but are calculated from the constructed scenario data, not sourced from a specific publication.
